{"id": "9:6/q12", "question": "What does hearing God's speech imply about its nature?", "turns_on": "Whether the audible recitation is the eternal attribute, created sounds, or a sign of a separate attribute.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q12/p1", "position": "The recited and heard Quran is genuinely God's speech, an eternal attribute rather than merely created text.", "reasons": "Tabrisi appeals to ordinary attribution of an author's speech across recitation; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin call the annexation an attribute to its described noun. Qurtubi cites Abu al-Hasan, al-Qadi Abu Bakr, al-Qalanisi, Ibn Mujahid and al-Isfarayini for hearing divine speech when recited, while affirming speech is not letters or sounds. Al-Ash'ari invokes the verse for hearing eternal speech."}, {"id": "9:6/q12/p2", "position": "Only originated letters and sounds are heard; therefore God's audible speech is created.", "reasons": "Razi and Abu Hayyan report the Mu'tazilite inference from successively produced audible sounds; Razi answers that present recitation is a human act even on their account and distinct from God's original production."}, {"id": "9:6/q12/p3", "position": "The very letters and sounds heard are eternal.", "reasons": "Razi attributes this to the Hashwiyya and reports others using 9:6 as evidence from what an idolater hears; he rejects identifying eternal speech with audible sound."}, {"id": "9:6/q12/p4", "position": "Hearing the recited letters also amounts to hearing a separate eternal speech.", "reasons": "Ibn Furak proposes this; Razi says other Ash'ari scholars reject it because no distinct entity beyond the sounds is heard."}, {"id": "9:6/q12/p5", "position": "One hears a sign conveying God's eternal attribute, not the attribute itself through the senses.", "reasons": "Abu Mansur rejects sensory hearing of the attribute; Bursevi uses the analogy of hearing news that indicates a person's knowledge. Alusi says hearing can be ascribed to a sign and that kalam can denote inward or voiced speech literally or figuratively, so the verse does not refute inner speech."}, {"id": "9:6/q12/p6", "position": "God's speech is a distinct entity persisting with every reader.", "reasons": "Razi reports al-Jubba'i's proposal and says the Mu'tazilites rejected it as unusual."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q13", "question": "Does the requirement to hear the Quran establish a proof for faith?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q13/p1", "position": "Hearing and considering the Quran supplies a binding miraculous proof; inquiry, rather than imitation, grounds faith.", "reasons": "Razi and Abu Hayyan infer the high rank of inquiry and insufficiency of imitation. Tabataba'i asks for certain knowledge, not strong probability. Al-Burhan and al-Itqan infer inimitability from the command to hear; al-Baqillani says eloquence, doubts, pride and attention explain varied listener responses. Tabari's discussion says unmatched eloquence is a messenger's proof, with speakers differing in capacity, citing 43:18 and works by al-Baqillani, al-Khattabi and al-Rummani. Al-Baqillani says the instruction to let the seeker hear shows recitation itself can establish proof against him. Bint al-Shati says its intended listeners need not be accomplished rhetoricians: early converts recognized inimitability through linguistic instinct, many later converts believed on first hearing after being kept from the Quran, and the eloquent miracle also confronted polytheists defending inherited religious, economic, and social arrangements."}, {"id": "9:6/q13/p2", "position": "The duty to explain proof extends to anyone seeking evidence or answers to religious doubts.", "reasons": "Razi extends protection by the stated reason of ignorance; Elmalili requires Muslims to explain divine unity and prophethood to a belligerent before killing, and to answer questions about affairs; Kuranyolu reports the duty for any non Muslim inquirer."}, {"id": "9:6/q13/p3", "position": "The verse rebuts the claim that religious knowledge is innate and necessary.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reasons that the people must hear and consider proofs precisely because they do not yet know them."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q14", "question": "How does hattā work in 'until he hears'?", "turns_on": "Whether hatta marks limit or purpose, and whether it may govern an unspoken pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q14/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'grant him protection' and can mark either an endpoint or a purpose.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and al-Samin allow both readings; the majority reject syntactic competition with istajāraka because it would force hatta to govern an omitted pronoun, tolerable only in poetic necessity. Alusi transmits the same objection."}, {"id": "9:6/q14/p2", "position": "It expresses purpose or cause: protect him so that he hears.", "reasons": "Alusi prefers this on context and the later requirement to send him safely away; Sari al-Din al-Misri says a merely terminal reading cannot account for protection after hearing."}, {"id": "9:6/q14/p3", "position": "With a grammatically permitted hidden pronoun, both verbs can compete to govern hattā.", "reasons": "Al-Samin reports grammarians who allow the omitted governed pronoun, comparing farḥtu wa marartu bi-Zayd."}]}
{"id": "9:6/q15", "question": "What must happen after the seeker has heard the message?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q15/p1", "position": "A non convert must remain unharmed and be returned or allowed to reach a safe place before hostilities resume.", "reasons": "Mujahid names the place he came from; Muqatil, Tha'labi and Baghawi permit fighting or killing if he later fights and is captured. Nasafi disallows harming, detaining, or letting him settle in Muslim territory. Biqa'i forbids betrayal before arrival. Tabataba'i stresses free choice; Asad cites 2:256. Ibn Ashur says this means release and non harm, without a duty to arrange escort or transport."}, {"id": "9:6/q15/p2", "position": "Acceptance of Islam places him within Muslim protection, so the return duty concerns refusal.", "reasons": "Wahidi says the convert becomes a brother in religion; al-Hasan says he enters Islam's protection; al-Dahhak and Sa'id ibn Abi Aruba say conversion is the desired outcome."}, {"id": "9:6/q15/p3", "position": "Once the proof has been established and he persists in rejection, fighting may be resumed after safe return.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i says killing is warranted only when hope of guidance ends; Kuranyolu says the later choice to leave the sacred zone or enter conflict is knowing and the kill restriction is geographically limited."}]}

{"id": "9:6/q18", "question": "What does maʾmanahu denote?", "turns_on": "Whether maʾman is a place noun or a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q18/p1", "position": "His safe place, normally his own people or homeland.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the possessive distinguishes the person's home safety from temporary asylum; Razi, as reported by Asad, glosses it as homeland. {"id": "9:6/q19", "question": "What does dhālika point back to?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative covers the whole process or a particular stage.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q19/p1", "position": "The kindness and whole sequence of granting asylum, allowing hearing, and securing return.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls these the acts of gentleness; Abu Hayyan reports him. {"id": "9:6/q20", "question": "What do 'they do not know' and its stated reason mean?", "turns_on": "The object of their ignorance and whether the clause explains teaching, return, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "9:6/q20/p1", "position": "They are ignorant of Islam, God's oneness, the message and its proofs; safety and teaching remove their excuse.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas glosses this as not reasoning; Maʾwardi also mentions not distinguishing guidance from error. {"id": "90:13/q06", "question": "How does the negation before this verse apply to freeing and feeding?", "turns_on": "Whether the preceding clause is straightforward negation or a rebuking omitted question.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q06/p1", "position": "One lā covers the coordinated deeds, although Arabic often repeats it.", "reasons": "Farra compares 75:31. {"id": "90:13/q07", "question": "What is the steep obstacle that this deed crosses?", "turns_on": "Whether the ascent is the morally difficult deed itself or a reported place beyond this life.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q07/p1", "position": "It is the difficult moral ascent of freeing, feeding, faith and other righteous deeds.", "reasons": "Majaz and Qatada identify its practical acts. {"id": "90:13/q09", "question": "Which is more virtuous, emancipation or charity?", "turns_on": "Whether precedence in the verse establishes comparative merit, against the companions' contrary ranking.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q09/p1", "position": "Emancipation is more virtuous.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and Sha'bi hold this; Sha'bi specifically prefers it to giving surplus to kin and cites the limb-for-limb promise. {"id": "90:13/q10", "question": "Which slave is best to free when price and faith differ?", "turns_on": "Whether the 'most costly' report includes an unbelieving slave or presumes a Muslim slave.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q10/p1", "position": "An expensive unbelieving slave is better to free than a cheap believing slave.", "reasons": "Asbagh invokes the Prophetic answer that the best slave to free is the most expensive."}, {"id": "90:13/q10/p2", "position": "A believing slave freed for worship and pure monotheism takes priority over mere price.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Arabi calls Asbagh mistaken: he takes the expensive-slave report to concern Muslims, citing reports about freeing a Muslim man and a believing slave. {"id": "90:13/q11", "question": "Why use 'release' here, and why place it first?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording stresses breadth of aid, the rank and difficulty of release, or the alternative ways of serving people.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q11/p1", "position": "The broad word 'release' includes even a small contribution toward another's freedom.", "reasons": "Biqai contrasts complete emancipation with helping pay; Samarrai contrasts fakk with the narrower taḥrīr used for expiation and includes debt and coercion."}, {"id": "90:13/q11/p2", "position": "Its first place marks emancipation as an especially important, difficult act of human service.", "reasons": "Samarrai says it emphasizes Islam's concern for liberation. Bint al-Shati calls it the first repair of human dignity, before wider social reform; Islahi says the good is universally recognized and early Qur'anic preaching later fostered gradual elimination of slavery. Bursevi says people spend on desires and buildings but begrudge a gift to the despised needy. Biqai connects the first pass to discipline of appetite, chastity and generosity."}, {"id": "90:13/q11/p3", "position": "The conjunction aw offers alternative acts of mercy rather than requiring them all together.", "reasons": "Samarrai says one may feed either needy class separately or both, and release or feeding gives a variety of possible routes."}]}
{"id": "90:13/q12", "question": "What does this deed teach about faith, wealth and social duty in the sūra?", "turns_on": "How emancipation and feeding relate to faith and mercy, and what their order implies.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q12/p1", "position": "Wealth should be spent on freeing and feeding the vulnerable as gratitude to God, with faith and mercy.", "reasons": "Kashshaf and Nasafi contrast this with boasting and waste; Baydawi calls the effort self-discipline. Corpus Coranicum links God's care and Meccan social and ritual life, and Samarrai says the boastful spender neglected the enslaved and hungry. Kur'an Yolu treats the list as examples of social ethics, not an exhaustive catalogue. Biqai calls for grateful compassion without display or reward-seeking. Elmalili extends liberation from one person to whole peoples."}, {"id": "90:13/q12/p2", "position": "The passage establishes human freedom as a foundational aim of Islamic law.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the Lawgiver strongly seeks freedom; Bint al-Shati says the first move toward dignity is ending slavery, and Islahi connects the early call to later gradual elimination."}, {"id": "90:13/q12/p3", "position": "Faith is a higher rank and a necessary ground for the deeds' acceptance.", "reasons": "Burhan takes thumma as rank, not time; Study Quran cites 9:54 for belief as a condition of acceptance. Ibn Khalawayh says the noun reading's actions are conditioned on faith."}, {"id": "90:13/q12/p4", "position": "Social justice precedes and grounds genuine faith in the sequence.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reads thumma temporally: emancipation and feeding first restore dignity and justice, enabling faith, patience and mercy. She rejects separating faith from resistance to tyranny, slavery and starvation."}, {"id": "90:13/q12/p5", "position": "The list echoes Isaiah and recasts heroic poetry through a call to protect the vulnerable.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum identifies Isaiah 58:5–7 and 58:6–7: both lists begin with slave release and move to the poor and kin, though the framing differs. It says the Qur'an grounds duty in God's grace rather than merely criticizing ritual, Arabizes the list, recalls 107:2–3, and challenges the poetic values mentioned at verse 6."}]}
{"id": "90:13/q13", "question": "What historical setting or examples illustrate freeing slaves here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q13/p1", "position": "The Meccan setting made slave release an urgent response to abused converts; Abu Bakr freed Bilal and six others.", "reasons": "Qutb says Muslims lacked a state and slavery was widespread. Corpus Coranicum connects worship with ordinary social support."}, {"id": "90:13/q13/p3", "position": "The preceding address may be read as the Prophet's direct address to the people.", "reasons": "Ibn Khalawayh records the preceding explanation and Kufan justification of an added alif by the closeness of simple and intensive verb forms."}]}

{"id": "90:13/q15", "question": "How does the teaching question about the obstacle work rhetorically?", "turns_on": "Whether the form itself guarantees an explanation, and how the question prepares the stated answer.", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q15/p1", "position": "The question creates curiosity and heightened tension before the answer in deeds.", "reasons": "Biqai says it stirs curiosity. {"id": "90:13/q16", "question": "What adjacent reading and vocabulary details do the commentaries record?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:13/q16/p1", "position": "Masghaba, maqraba and matraba evoke hunger, kinship and dust-poverty.", "reasons": "Samīn reports al-Raghib's 'hunger with fatigue,' sometimes thirst with fatigue, and al-Zamakhshari's matching derivations from hunger, closeness and poverty. Samīn adds that tariba is poverty with skin touching dust, whereas atraba means becoming rich."}, {"id": "90:13/q16/p2", "position": "Abu Jaʿfar reads the earlier labadan with gemination while others read it lightly.", "reasons": "Tabarisi records this neighboring reading without tying it to a different interpretation of freeing."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q01", "question": "How does this clause connect grammatically with the earlier failed ascent?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier negative or an implied question governs this clause, and whether an ellipsis is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q01/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with 'he did not cross the ascent,' so the rebuke also denies his faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān attach it to 90:11; al-Ālūsī prefers the negative reading, saying the repeated negation singles out faith as the noblest part of the ascent, not something outside it. Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise infer that the rebuked man neither crossed nor believed; al-Zajjāj says the second clause shows his unbelief."}, {"id": "90:17/q01/p2", "position": "The earlier lā may be read as a prayer, an urging question, or with an omitted interrogative.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya records denial, exhortation, and prayer as readings of 90:11. Al-Ālūsī attributes alternatives to Ibn Zayd, al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim and objects on grammatical grounds; grammarians criticize a line by ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa used for omitted interrogative hamza."}, {"id": "90:17/q01/p3", "position": "The phrase can be supplied as 'then his being among the believers.'", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī compares 3:86, where he understands an omitted conjunction before 'they testified.'"}]}
{"id": "90:17/q02", "question": "Why is one negative lā used across the coordinated ascent clauses?", "turns_on": "Whether customary repetition is required.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q02/p1", "position": "One lā can cover the connected clauses; repetition is usual but not obligatory.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says the single negation covers freeing, feeding, and believing though Arabic commonly repeats it, comparing 75:31. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says instances of repetition do not prove a rule; al-Ālūsī cites 25:67 and poetry via al-Ṭībī and allows omission."}, {"id": "90:17/q02/p2", "position": "A repeated negative is grammatically expected.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports al-Zajjāj's objection, which al-Fārisī answers; al-Farrāʾ describes repetition as normal usage."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q03", "question": "What does thumma convey between the good deeds and faith?", "turns_on": "Whether thumma orders time, rank, expression, conjunction, or the believer's final state; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ makes social deeds a prior ground of faith.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q03/p1", "position": "It marks faith's higher rank, not later time.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Burhān, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Quṭb and al-Sāmarrāʾī say faith precedes or validates deeds. Al-Ālūsī adds that faith alone can save before duties fall due. Quṭb says faith grounds action in a stable divine way rather than whim or praise. Al-Qāshānī and al-Bursawī present the rise from generosity/chastity to wisdom, patience/courage and mercy/justice. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports but rejects this detachment of faith from social deeds."}, {"id": "90:17/q03/p2", "position": "It orders the mention or wording, while faith already existed when the deeds were done.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī cite a poem that names a son's eminence before his father and grandfather though the elders attained it first. Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Itqān and al-Sāmarrāʾī likewise distinguish report order from event order; the Ḥamāsa commentator says thumma can delay words but need not delay clauses."}, {"id": "90:17/q03/p3", "position": "Here it functions like 'and,' joining faith to freeing and feeding without temporal order.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī and al-Itqān report this reading. Al-Jishumī adds that faith encompasses obedience. Al-Burhān argues that a rank reading removes the perceived need to replace thumma with 'and.'"}, {"id": "90:17/q03/p4", "position": "It can mark later faith after deeds performed before conversion.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Biqāʿī allow a beneficent pre-Islamic person to believe later; the Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām report supports the reception of earlier good. Al-Biqāʿī describes a later second ascent that purifies reason. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers real sequence, making emancipation and feeding prerequisites for sincere social faith."}, {"id": "90:17/q03/p5", "position": "It can indicate the person's final state: he remained faithful until death.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn make dying in faith a condition for earlier deeds' benefit; al-Qurṭubī compares 20:82."}, {"id": "90:17/q03/p6", "position": "It marks a real sequence in which freeing and feeding establish the social ground for faith.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says a society accepting slavery and starvation cannot sustain genuine faith; she objects to readings that separate belief from resisting tyranny and neglect of the poor. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ argues that thumma's plain sense marks order with delay and that non-temporal readings strain the passage; she connects the sequence to 107:1–2, where rejecting Judgment appears in repelling the orphan and failing to urge feeding the poor."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q04", "question": "What is the role of faith in the acceptance of the earlier deeds?", "turns_on": "Whether faith must accompany deeds, can validate good from before conversion, or includes confidence in the deeds' value.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q04/p1", "position": "Faith is required for freeing and feeding to count as a successful ascent or receive reward.", "reasons": "Muqātil says duties without faith do not secure acceptance of charity and expiation. Ibn Kathīr adds inward belief, intention for God's reward, 17:19 and 16:97. Quṭb says faith connects action to a divine norm. Al-Ālūsī adds that faith alone can save before obligations arise."}, {"id": "90:17/q04/p2", "position": "If the person later accepts Islam, earlier good done for God can come forward with that faith.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr invoke the Prophet's reply to Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the deeds are praised and rewarded as though done in Islam; al-Biqāʿī says later faith embraces them. Al-Qurṭubī separately denies benefit when belief arrives merely after spending, appealing to 9:54."}, {"id": "90:17/q04/p3", "position": "Belief here can mean conviction that the good deeds are beneficial and necessary before God.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the view that the doer believes the deeds will benefit him with God. {"id": "90:17/q06", "question": "Who exemplifies the believers described here?", "turns_on": "Whether the text is illustrated by exemplary Companions or read as a rebuke of the boastful man.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q06/p1", "position": "The foremost Companions, including the four caliphs, are examples.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī names Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf; al-Rāzī says the leading Companions including four caliphs were patient in religion and merciful to people."}, {"id": "90:17/q06/p2", "position": "Abū Bakr is the exemplary case, including his noble conduct before conversion.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī ranks him immediately after prophets, citing Ibn al-Dughunnah's praise of kinship, hospitality, helping the burdened and distressed, Khadīja's similar reassurance to the Prophet, his swift conversion, his response at Ḥudaybiyya matching the Prophet's words, and his refusal of wine to preserve reason."}, {"id": "90:17/q06/p3", "position": "It addresses the boastful spender, contrasting his failure with the believers' path.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī identifies the man who boasted of spending much; al-Nasafī says he failed to thank the Benefactor by freeing, feeding and believing. {"id": "90:17/q07", "question": "What does tawāṣaw require of believers?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis falls on mutual support, public moral guidance, or the counselors' own practice.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q07/p1", "position": "They advise and strengthen one another in good, sharing responsibility for patience and mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī glosses it as mutual advice. {"id": "90:17/q08", "question": "What patience do believers urge one another to have?", "turns_on": "Which demand for self-command is emphasized: worship, faith, abstention, trial, or the hardships surrounding the ascent.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q08/p1", "position": "Patience in obeying God and carrying out His obligations.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Tustarī say obedience; Hishām ibn Ḥassān, Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil specify obligations and Quranic commands. {"id": "90:17/q09", "question": "What does marḥama mean, and to whom does it extend?", "turns_on": "Whether marḥama denotes human compassion, particular recipients or kin, acts attracting divine mercy, or the merciful next life.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q09/p1", "position": "Compassion and merciful action toward people and other creatures, including fellow believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly says all people; Tustarī says creatures, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya says mutual care sustains human life. Al-Māwardī includes one another and everyone. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Ālūsī and others give the broad gloss.
